description: Lambda functions must not include sensitive data in environment variables

requirements.description: Lambda function has no Environment property at all (no environment variables defined).
requirements.rationale: If there are no environment variables, there cannot be any sensitive data exposure via environment variables. The rule has nothing to evaluate.

requirements.description: Lambda function has Environment.Variables set to an empty object/map.
requirements.rationale: An empty Variables map contains no keys or values, so no sensitive data can be present.

requirements.description: Lambda function has environment variables containing only benign, non-sensitive keys (e.g., LOG_LEVEL=INFO, REGION=us-east-1, STAGE=prod, TABLE_NAME=my-table).
requirements.rationale: Lambda environment variables are intended to hold non-sensitive configuration. AWS docs explicitly endorse this use (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/simplify-serverless-applications-with-environment-variables-in-aws-lambda/). None of these keys match a sensitive-key pattern.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable with a key matching a sensitive pattern (e.g., PASSWORD, DB_PASSWORD, SECRET, API_KEY, ACCESS_KEY, TOKEN, PRIVATE_KEY, CREDENTIALS) and a literal hard-coded string value.
requirements.rationale: AWS docs state: 'For sensitive information like database credentials or API keys, AWS recommends using AWS Secrets Manager instead of environment variables' (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-envvars.html). A sensitive-named key with a literal string value indicates a plaintext secret in the environment. Mirrors ECS_NO_ENVIRONMENT_SECRETS Config rule semantics.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable with a benign key name (e.g., CONFIG_VALUE, RANDOM_ID) whose VALUE is a high-entropy string that resembles a secret.
requirements.rationale: Per resolved decision, the rule uses key-name pattern matching only (mirroring AWS Config's ecs-no-environment-secrets behavior with its secretKeys parameter). Pure value-content/entropy analysis is not performed because it produces too many false positives (random IDs, hashes, etc.).

requirements.description: Lambda function has multiple environment variables; at least one has a sensitive-named key with a literal string value while others are benign.
requirements.rationale: A single sensitive variable is sufficient to violate the rule. Mirrors ECS_NO_ENVIRONMENT_SECRETS: NON_COMPLIANT if 1 or more keys match. The presence of benign variables does not offset the exposure of any single secret.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable whose key is sensitive-sounding (e.g., API_KEY, DB_PASSWORD) but whose value is a CloudFormation Ref or Fn::GetAtt to another resource (e.g., a Secrets Manager Secret, an SSM Parameter, or any other resource in the template).
requirements.rationale: Per resolved decision, Ref/GetAtt indicates the value is computed at deploy time from another managed resource rather than being a hard-coded secret in the template. Treating these as compliant aligns with the AWS-recommended pattern of injecting references rather than literal secrets.

requirements.description: Lambda function's environment variable value is a CloudFormation dynamic reference such as '{{resolve:secretsmanager:MySecret:SecretString:password}}' or '{{resolve:ssm-secure:MyParam}}'.
requirements.rationale: Per resolved decision, dynamic references are an AWS-documented pattern (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/creating-aws-lambda-environmental-variables-from-aws-secrets-manager/). The template itself contains no secret material; the resolution happens at deploy time using IAM-controlled access.

requirements.description: Lambda function's environment variable value is an unresolvable intrinsic function (e.g., Fn::ImportValue from another stack, Fn::If with unknown condition branches, Fn::Sub with unresolvable parameters).
requirements.rationale: When the value is an unresolvable intrinsic, the rule cannot statically assert the value contains a literal secret. Avoiding false positives on unknowable values is a core principle of static analysis.

requirements.description: Lambda function's entire Environment property is wrapped in an Fn::If whose branches are not statically resolvable.
requirements.rationale: If the rule cannot determine which environment configuration will be deployed, it cannot assert non-compliance.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable named with a sensitive-sounding key but the value is an empty string ''.
requirements.rationale: An empty string is still a literal value (not a Ref/GetAtt or dynamic reference). The key-name match indicates intent to place a credential in the environment, and the literal value confirms the variable is being assigned in the template. Mirrors ECS_NO_ENVIRONMENT_SECRETS' key-name-driven semantics.

requirements.description: Resource is not a Lambda function (e.g., AWS::ECS::TaskDefinition, AWS::Batch::JobDefinition) even though it also has environment variables containing sensitive-sounding keys.
requirements.rationale: This rule is scoped to Lambda functions only. Other resource types with environment variables are evaluated by separate rules (e.g., ecs-no-environment-secrets).

requirements.description: Lambda function has KmsKeyArn configured for environment variable encryption, but still contains a sensitive-named environment variable with a literal hard-coded string value.
requirements.rationale: KMS encryption at rest does not change that the value is hard-coded in the template/state and visible to anyone with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration permission. AWS guidance is unambiguous: do not store secrets in environment variables (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/securely-retrieving-secrets-with-aws-lambda/).

requirements.description: Lambda function (Terraform aws_lambda_function) has an environment block with variables = {} (explicit empty map).
requirements.rationale: Equivalent to no environment variables — no sensitive data can be present.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable whose key name contains a sensitive token as a substring (e.g., MY_APP_SECRET_VALUE, USER_PASSWORD_HASH, AUTH_TOKEN_HEADER) with a literal string value.
requirements.rationale: Substring matches against well-known sensitive tokens (password, secret, token, key, credential, passphrase) should be flagged. This mirrors common implementations of AWS Config's secretKeys parameter and standard DLP key-name matching.

requirements.description: Lambda function declares Environment.Variables with sensitive-named keys whose values are explicitly null (e.g., Variables: { PASSWORD: null }).
requirements.rationale: Null values do not constitute sensitive data exposure — there is no literal secret material in the template. The variable is effectively unset.

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable with a sensitive-sounding key but with a comment-style placeholder value such as 'CHANGEME', 'REPLACE_ME', or 'TODO'.
requirements.rationale: Placeholder strings are still literal values present in the template, and the sensitive key name signals intent to store a credential. The rule should not whitelist placeholder values; rather, the proper fix is to use Secrets Manager or SSM (Ref/GetAtt or dynamic reference).

requirements.description: Lambda function has an environment variable with key 'AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID' or 'AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' set to a literal string value.
requirements.rationale: These are explicitly sensitive credential keys. Additionally, AWS Lambda reserves these names and embedding literals here is both insecure and may conflict with the function's execution role credentials. Strong key-name match.
